::: {.why}
Price data is rarely restated and fundamental data routinely is, so any signal built on reported numbers is using a value that did not exist on the day the backtest says it traded.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Say what point-in-time means for a fundamental item, and name the three dates every such item needs.
- Estimate the size of the restatement effect using your one worked example and the reporting lag distribution.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Read the SEC financial statement data sets documentation as far as understanding the file structure and the ADSH accession identifier, which is what lets you tie a number to the filing that reported it rather than to the period it describes.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Design the schema you would need: fiscal period end, filing date, and ingestion date, with the query returning the latest filing whose filing date precedes the as-of date. Write the SQL, using the same pattern as day 19's as-of query, and note the one extra complication, which is that a later filing can restate an earlier period.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Measure the lag distribution: for a sample of filings, report the median and 90th percentile days between fiscal period end and filing date. That distribution is the minimum lag any fundamental signal must respect.
:::
:::
